description: Predictive global pathway with only today's legislated energy policies enacted.
pathwayDescription: The Current Policies Scenario (CPS) offers a cautious view of the energy sector’s trajectory. It considers only policies and regulations already adopted in legislation, assumes no change even where governments have signalled an intention to act, and takes the lower end of any target range. Time-bound policies are not extended once they expire, and new energy technologies are assumed to be deployed and integrated more slowly than in recent years. Under these conditions, oil and natural gas demand keep growing to mid-century, and global energy-related CO2 emissions stay close to 40 Gt per year through 2050. The CPS pathway corresponds to 2.9°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability), compared with 2.5°C in the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) and a return to below 1.5°C by 2100 in the IEA’s Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario (NZE).

coreDrivers.policies: The CPS holds today's legislated and regulated energy policies fixed. No new measures are added, and where existing policies target a range of outcomes the lower end is assumed. Time-bound policies (e.g. tax credits, mandates with an expiry date) are not renewed or strengthened once they lapse, even where governments have signalled further action.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Falling unit costs for solar PV and battery storage continue to support their expansion even without new policy support, driving most incremental power capacity. Higher-cost or still-immature low-carbon options (CCUS, green hydrogen) see markedly slower deployment than in the acoompanying STEPS/NZE under CPS's 'generally cautious perspective on the speed at which new energy technologies are deployed'.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-emissions technologies' share of total energy investment rises only marginally, to about 70% in 2035. Spending stays tilted toward maintaining conventional supply: oil and gas supply investment rises about 7% over 2025-2035.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP growth are common assumptions across all three WEO-2025 scenarios (global GDP CAGR 2024-2050 = 2.6%; population rising from 8.09 to 9.57 billion). In the CPS specifically, where no new policy or technology-breakthrough assumption operates, these demographic and macroeconomic trends are the primary driver of the modelled increase in energy service demand (TFC +32.4% 2024-2050).

dependencies.dependency_description: CPS models no new decarbonisation, CCUS, or hydrogen policy support beyond what is already legislated. Continued renewables deployment to 2050 rests mainly on cost economics rather than policy strategy support.
Slow grid integration and permitting/market constraints materially slow renewables and storage deployment in the power sector.
CO2 prices in the CPS stay flat and low across regions, providing limited economic pull for low-carbon generation beyond underlying technology cost declines.
Nuclear capacity roughly doubles even under CPS's cautious technology-adoption assumption, implying siting and public-acceptance conditions are assumed at least neutral.
Demand-side flexibility and smart charging are helpful but less binding in CPS because end-use electrification is slower than STEPS/NZE.
Battery storage capacity grows substantially in CPS to help integrate a rising renewables share, but grid/transmission expansion is not separately quantified in this dataset for CPS.

CPS's generally cautious perspective on the speed at which new energy technologies are deployed' means CCUS, hydrogen/ammonia and SMR generation remain small shares of the mix by 2050, consistent with slower assumed progress on technologies not yet fully market-ready.
Critical-mineral supply concentration risk applies to batteries and solar.
Higher long-run warming raises weather-related reliability risks for power grids, thermal plants, hydropower and cooling-driven peaks.
The pathway implies grid, storage and generation workforce needs, but the attached report does not provide pathway-specific labor bottlenecks for Power.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Combustion emissions from the electricity and heat sectors are combined. Upstream (fuel extraction/processing) emissions are not included. This includes global aggregate power-system output, there is no separate captive or residential-rooftop generation series.

Combustion emissions from the electricity and heat sectors are combined. Upstream (fuel extraction/processing) emissions are not included. This includes global aggregate power-system output, there is no separate captive or residential-rooftop generation series.
Storage figure is battery storage capacity only, there is no separate pumped-hydro-storage series in this dataset.

Coal and natural gas are further split by 'unabated' and 'with-CCUS' in the source data. Solar combines Solar PV and concentrating solar power. 'Other' includes Marine and Hydrogen/H2-based generation.
